name: Adropin
lead: Adropin is a 76-amino-acid peptide encoded by the ENHO gene, reported in 2008 in Cell Metabolism as a secreted factor linking dietary macronutrient intake with energy homeostasis and lipid metabolism in mice.[1][2] Its name combines Latin words for 'set fire to' and 'fat'.[2] That name, and the animal findings behind it, are why it appears in discussions of fat loss and body composition: in mice, higher adropin goes with leanness and better glucose and fat handling, so it is sometimes discussed as a possible lever on body fat.[3][4]

It is made mainly in the liver and brain. Animal studies report effects on glucose tolerance, fat use, endothelial function and physical activity, while human data consist mostly of blood-level associations with obesity, ageing and cardiometabolic disease.[3][4][5][6][7] Adropin is an endogenous peptide; it has no approved therapeutic use, and no published human trial has tested it as a treatment for body fat or appearance.
infobox: Liver, brain (highest in hypothalamus), heart, gut[2]
Latin aduro (set fire to) and pinguis (fat)[2]

paras: Adropin was identified by a research group led by Andrew Butler, whose 2008 paper in Cell Metabolism described a secreted protein encoded by a gene named Energy Homeostasis Associated (Enho), expressed in liver and brain.[1][2] In that paper liver Enho expression was regulated by nutrition: it rose rapidly in lean mice given a high-fat diet and fell with fasting, but declined in mice that had become obese over months of high-fat feeding.[1]

Follow-up papers broadened its profile. A 2010 Circulation paper reported that adropin acts on endothelial cells and in a mouse vascular injury model, positioning it as a regulator of endothelial function.[6] A 2012 Obesity paper reported that adropin deficiency in mice is associated with higher adiposity and insulin resistance, and that serum levels respond to diet and metabolic state.[3] A 2012 human study reported low circulating levels with obesity and ageing, rising after gastric bypass surgery.[7] Reviews in 2014 and 2016 grouped adropin with other newly described peptides such as preptin and irisin as 'new players' in energy regulation.[13][22]
The peptide is highly conserved across mammals and is expressed most strongly in the brain, as well as in the liver, heart and gut. Liver expression follows feeding status.[2]

Mice lacking adropin showed increased adiposity and insulin resistance.[3] Treatment improved glucose tolerance and substrate use in diet-induced obese mice.[4] A separate mouse study reported a role in physical activity via NB-3/Notch signalling,[5] and another reported effects on endothelial function.[6]

Adropin is cleaved from a larger precursor encoded by ENHO, a gene on human chromosome 9. It is highly conserved across mammals, with the strongest expression in the brain (particularly the hypothalamus) and also in liver, heart and gut. Its liver expression depends on feeding status, dietary macronutrients and the body clock.[2] The orphan receptor GPR19 has been proposed as an adropin receptor, partly on the basis of a 2016 study of drinking behaviour in animals; receptors remain an active research question.[2]

In metabolic experiments, adropin treatment improved glucose tolerance and substrate use in diet-induced obese mice,[4] and a Redox Biology paper reported protection against liver injury in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis in a model through Nrf2-mediated antioxidant capacity.[20] Reviews place adropin among hepatokines, liver-secreted proteins whose release follows feeding and which signal to brain, heart, pancreas and fat tissue.[23] Other reported effects include a role in physical activity through the NB-3/Notch pathway in the mouse brain,[5] vascular protection via endothelial nitric oxide synthase,[6][11] and, per Wikipedia, regulation by oestrogen in the liver, which may explain sex differences seen in some human data.[2]

Reviews summarise work on adropin in cardiovascular disease, including associations with atherosclerosis and hypertension,[12] and in neurological conditions, including stroke and cognitive decline, where it is described as protective in animal models and linked to blood-brain barrier integrity.[11] A Nature Reviews Rheumatology highlight describes an animal and human-tissue study in which adropin reduced fibroblast activation and fibrosis relevant to systemic sclerosis, a condition affecting skin.[21] Adropin deficiency was reported to worsen experimental colitis in mice.[24] In each case the work is preclinical or observational.

Low circulating adropin has been reported with obesity and ageing, and levels were reported to rise after gastric bypass surgery.[7] Low serum adropin has also been associated with coronary atherosclerosis.[8] These are associations and do not establish cause.

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 observational studies (2,813 participants) found serum adropin significantly lower in people with type 2 diabetes than in controls, with very high heterogeneity between studies.[14] Studies of diet found that fasting plasma adropin correlated with fat consumption in women,[15] and that plasma adropin responded differently to dietary glucose and fructose.[16] These are measurements of the body's own peptide, not tests of giving it as a drug.

No studies found testing adropin as a treatment for appearance or body composition. Registered human studies are observational, measuring serum adropin in conditions such as chronic liver disease, periodontal disease and obesity.[9][10]

Several randomised trials have measured adropin as a biomarker outcome of other interventions. A trial in older adults examined how aerobic exercise training changes nitric oxide-related hormones including adropin over time,[17] another assessed a multicomponent exercise programme on adropin, endothelial function, insulin resistance and sleep in overweight older adults,[18] and a 2025 trial in adults with metabolic syndrome tested partial replacement of animal with plant protein and tracked serum adropin among its outcomes.[19] ClinicalTrials.gov also lists observational registrations measuring adropin in obese men alongside testosterone and adiponectin, and in periodontitis and chronic liver disease.[9][10]

card.summary: A liver and brain peptide linked to fat metabolism in mice; human data are blood-level associations only.
card.note: Endogenous peptide; no approved use or human treatment trials found.

quick.overview:
Adropin is a small peptide made mostly in the liver and brain. In mice, low levels go with more body fat and insulin resistance, and giving it improved glucose handling.
In people, lower blood levels have been associated with obesity and heart disease, but no trials test adropin as a way to change body fat or appearance.
quick.mechanism: It is cleaved from the ENHO gene product, and its expression follows feeding and the body clock. The receptor is not fully established; GPR19 has been proposed.
quick.risks: No approved product exists and no human safety data for administering it have been reported.

chain: Adropin signalling is linked in mice to fat use and insulin sensitivity
Leaner body composition and better glucose handling in animal models
Possible relevance to fat loss and a leaner look
angle.text: Adropin is discussed because mice with more of it are leaner and metabolically healthier, and low levels in people go along with obesity. It remains a research peptide: its connection to how someone looks is a hypothesis drawn from animal studies and blood-level associations.
